title: The one he loved (John 13:18–30)
hook: the beloved disciple leans on his chest; Judas goes out, and it was night

segments.voice: Yesterday, a towel and a basin, and Jesus washing every disciple's feet. Your line was to the end.

Forget the famous painting. In Leonardo's Last Supper, everyone sits in a row on one side of a long table, like a panel at a conference. At a formal dinner in Jesus's world, guests often reclined: low couches around a low table, each guest propped on one elbow, feet stretched out behind. Your head was near your neighbor's chest. Jesus has just washed their feet. Now, deeply troubled, he says something that stops the meal.

"Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." The disciples look at each other, not knowing whom he means. And John introduces someone he hasn't named this way before: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." The beloved disciple. John's Gospel never gives his name. He appears at the cross, at the empty tomb, by the lake, and at the very end the Gospel says this disciple is the one who wrote these things down. Who was he? Church tradition, as early as Irenaeus, says John, the son of Zebedee. Some modern scholars suggest someone else: Lazarus, whom the sisters called he whom thou lovest, or a disciple from Jerusalem outside the twelve. Nobody can prove it. The Gospel keeps his name quiet, maybe on purpose, so any reader can lean into that place. An echo: the word for bosom is the one used in chapter one, where the Son is in the bosom of the Father. As Jesus rests close to the Father, this disciple rests close to Jesus. Peter nudges him: ask who it is. He leans back and asks. Jesus answers: the one I give this dipped bread to. And he gives it to Judas. Some readers see the morsel as a host's mark of honor; if so, even now, Jesus offers him friendship. Then: "That thou doest, do quickly." The others think Judas is going to buy something for the feast, or give to the poor. And John ends the scene: "He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night."

Let your body lean into whatever is holding you, the back of a chair, a wall, the floor, and notice how much effort you usually spend holding yourself up. Then think of a person you trust enough to lean on, and picture leaning on them a little, the way the beloved disciple leaned back to ask a hard question. If you pray, rest in God the same way; if not, simply let yourself be held.
Beloved disciple. The unnamed disciple whom Jesus loved, who leaned on his chest at supper, and whom John's Gospel names as its witness.
Your line: and it was night. Judas goes out, and the door closes behind him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians remember this supper on Maundy or Holy Thursday; church tradition honors the beloved disciple as Saint John the Evangelist, while some scholars hold the question of his identity open.

chat.says: Who was the disciple Jesus loved? Do we actually know his name?
options: John's Gospel never names him. Tradition says John; some scholars suggest Lazarus.
John's Gospel names him plainly as Peter, the one who leaned close at supper.
John's Gospel says it was Judas, the friend Jesus loved even as he left.
chat.meaning: John's Gospel never gives his name. Church tradition, as early as Irenaeus, says John, son of Zebedee; some modern scholars suggest Lazarus or someone else.

notes: Index word is 'beloved disciple'; title 'The one he loved'. Kept.
First explicit 'disciple whom Jesus loved' is 13:23 (some suggest the unnamed disciple of 1:35–40). Script says 'someone we've never been told about before'; confirm.
Identity: Irenaeus (c. 180) identifies the disciple who leaned on Jesus's breast as John. Lazarus proposal (from 11:3, 5, 36) and others. Confirm.
Reclining posture at formal meals (triclinium-style); confirm.
The morsel as a mark of honor: common commentary claim; confirm.
Leonardo's Last Supper mentioned descriptively, not as error.
